clips.title: DORA Metrics Explained
clips.why: Two of the delivery numbers our job computes, change lead time and change failure rate, explained by people who build a tool that measures them.
look: Where change lead time starts and where it stops: our job starts at the first commit and stops at the merge.
What counts as a failed change. Ours: a revert, a hotfix or a Bug fix that touches the PR's lines within 14 days.
Listen for why speed alone is not enough, and keep it in mind for the dashboards lesson: speed and failure belong in the same picture.
clips.after: Our job writes both numbers per team and week, and the delivery dashboard never shows merged PRs without change failure next to them.

clips.title: How Sleuth measures Change Lead Time
clips.why: Lead time cut into buckets, one of which, review lag, is almost exactly our review wait.
look: The four buckets of a pull request's life: coding, waiting for review, being reviewed, deploying.
Review lag: the time a PR waits before anyone looks at it. That is the number Nova's work should change.
Each bucket needs a timestamp from the PR's history, which is why our query asks for the timeline events.
clips.after: Our review wait is the review-lag bucket: from ready for review to the first review by a person, read from the timeline GitHub keeps forever.

clips.title: DORA Metrics Explained
clips.why: A short warning about using these numbers the right way, which is the reason our job only ever writes team numbers.
look: Listen for who the numbers are meant for, and what they are meant to help with.
Ask yourself what would change if these numbers were shown per person instead of per team.
clips.after: That is why every series carries a team and never a login, and why a team of two is reported as "other".

practice.q: A PR opened as a draft on Monday 09:00, became ready for review on Monday 13:00, Byte reviewed it at 13:10 and Dana at Tuesday 09:00. What is its review wait?

options.why: That starts at opening. A draft is not waiting for anyone, so the clock starts when it becomes ready for review.
Byte is a bot. Its review does not end a person's wait for another person.
From ready for review (Monday 13:00) to the first review by a person who is not the author (Tuesday 09:00).

practice.q: Finish the line the job pushes for the week of Monday 31 August 2026, so it lands on that week and not on the night the job ran.
practice.hint: Milliseconds since 1970 for 2026-08-31T00:00:00Z. The lab prints it.
practice.why: The timestamp at the end of the line says which week the number describes. Without it, the database stamps the arrival time, and a whole backfill lands on one night.

practice.q: Your backfill pushes 12 weeks to a fresh VictoriaMetrics, curl prints 204, and the dashboard is empty. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The retention period is shorter than the oldest week, so those points were dropped
options.why: The default keeps one month. Older points are counted in vm_rows_ignored_total and never stored, while the request still answers 204.

options.text: The values are medians, and the dashboard only draws counters
options.why: A dashboard draws any stored number. Medians are drawn as they are, without rate().

options.text: GitHub's search returned more than 1000 results
options.why: That would lose some PRs inside a week, not every point of every week. The job asks one week at a time to avoid it anyway.

practice.q: Put one night of the metrics job in order.
items: The cron starts the job at 02:20
The job asks GitHub for last week's PRs with their timeline events
It keeps the raw answers as a JSON file of the run
It computes review wait per PR and the medians per team
It pushes one line per team and number, stamped with last week's Monday
practice.why: Raw data is kept before any formula runs, so a mistake in a formula can be fixed by recomputing, and the timestamp is the week, not the night.

practice.q: In September nobody had an agent, so there were no agent PRs. What should the job write for "agent PRs merged" in September?

options.why: A 0 before October and a real value after it draws a sudden jump that looks like an improvement.

options.text: Nothing, so the chart shows no data before October
options.why: "No data" is the truth: the number did not exist yet. A chart then starts the line where the agents start.

options.text: The human merge rate, as a stand-in
options.why: That mixes two cohorts and makes the agent line meaningless.
